candidates.worst_problem: At 1600x900 and 1280x800 the Blanket Fort frame hovers over the floor with nothing holding it, its candle shelf ends in air, and the rug below does not touch it, so the left half has no contact.
At both sizes the carved pedestal finally carries the frame, but the wall above it stays a near-empty dark band, and the plum rug is cut off by the bottom edge, more tightly at 1280x800.
At both sizes the floor under the frame and along the bottom is a dim, nearly empty void, so the frame floats with no contact and the room reads as unfinished.

The red-and-blue rug and striped fringe at lower left read as a noisy, over-saturated repeat at both sizes and are the first thing to look procedural; repaint them darker and woven, and give the thin console legs more mass under the frame.

The window shafts at both sides are stiff hatched blocks of pale grey that sit on top of the wainscot rather than lighting it, most obviously at 1600x900, and the parchment's straight lower sides still read as a panel.
The moonlight falls in a curved drape-like shape that does not follow the window's angle before its bright pool at floor level, and the upper wall stays dark and undescribed at both sizes.
At both sizes the moonlight ends as soft airbrushed cones that fade before landing on wainscot or floor, and the parchment's ruler-straight ruled edges read as a CSS panel.

The moonlight across the wainscot is too faint and muddy to read as a cold shaft against the warm panelling at both sizes, and the magenta wall drifts brighter than the samples' aubergine, so cool the wall and strengthen the shaft where it crosses the rail and floor.

The left pillar and shrine dissolve into dark at both sizes, leaving the outer board margins plainer than the alcove; the dark cost disk on the card and the row badges are clear but could carry more worn gold.
The pale tan leather rules panel on the central card is a large, flat, off-palette block at both sizes, and the plate under the card spreads wider than the card and fights the shrine.
The shrine is a hard-edged pasted rectangle at both sizes, with a flat pale cost disk, streaky bright purple rows, and FROM YOUR FINAL DECK crowding the ends of its narrow plate.

The pillars stop well below the card and carry odd long hanging wires, so the card stands in front of a shrine too small for it at both sizes, and the smudged dark trick rows have plainer ends than the card's ornament.
The dark cost disks are legible but read as flat coins with thin rims at both sizes, and the TRICKS lettering on the ribbon sinks into its tan at 1600x900 and is dim at 1280x800.
The worn cost disks swallow their numerals, the flat blue-grey leather body panels are large and off-palette, and Mr. Moth's plate sits detached below the shelf at 1600x900.
The shelf band cuts through Mr. Moth's nameplate at 1600x900 and it sits muddily on the shelf at 1280x800, while the large flat pale cost disks shout like CSS circles over the worn rims.
Mr. Moth's nameplate is separated from his portrait by the shelf at 1600x900 and hangs at the shelf's end at 1280x800, though the worn gold cost disks are the best of the four.
The plaque lettering is still pale and slightly cold against the room's warm light at both sizes; warm the highlight and add a gold under-edge so it stops looking laid over the painting.
The dark engraved lettering belongs to the room but loses too much contrast against its plaques, so WEAK, STRENGTH and VULNERABLE read poorly at 1600x900 and worse at 1280x800.
The purple-filled plates and saturated cyan and pink letters glow like an overlay rather than taking the room's warm light at both sizes, despite being very legible.
The condition plaques are plain gold-outlined rectangles at both sizes, the one element here that reads as a web tag rather than a sample cartouche; give them shaped scrolled ends.

verdicts.verdict: No candidate reaches reference fit: coherence stays below 9 on every screen, at both 1600x900 and 1280x800. JASPER is my system winner, though it is close with CITRINE and takes only rest and event. Its drawn wall, wainscot, floor and rug give the board screens a real room, and that carries to gameover and shop, which matters more than its fixable faults: rectangular combat plaques, a faint moon shaft and a loud rug. CITRINE wins gameover, shop and combat on ornament and staging, but its rest frame floats and its event moon shafts are stiff, so its best parts should be grafted into JASPER. MALACHITE has the best parchment and a strong pedestal, but its leather card panels and dim plaque lettering hurt it. SERPENTINE is last on four of five screens because of its empty floor, moon cones, pasted shrine, flat pale cost disks and the shelf cutting through the nameplate.

candidates.worst_problem: The fort frame touches nothing: its plaque shelf hangs in the air above a fringed rug, and the upper wall stays a dark smear with no drawn architecture (1600: gap reads clearly; 1280: rug crowds the plaque but stays clean).

The lower-left rug and striped floor strip are more saturated and harsher than the damask and wainscot above, so the floor stops matching the wall (1600: striped band at bottom-left looks like a different texture; 1280: rug red still competes with the fort painting).
The band under the fort frame and choices is an empty dark floor with no rug, stand or contact, leaving the frame floating over nothing (visible at both 1600 and 1280).

The carved pedestal and purple rug ground the frame well, but the wall behind stays a dim ochre-and-violet haze with no wainscot detail (1600: wall is the weak half; 1280: rug is cut low and the pedestal carries the floor alone).

The moonlight beams are hard grey striped slabs pasted across the wainscot, reading as an overlay rather than light on wood, and the floor pools are cut off by a near-black floor (1600: stripes dominate the sides; 1280: pools stay flat grey).

The moon shafts are too faint and cross into muddy X shapes on the wainscot, so the stone pools look unconnected to the windows, and the damask wall runs magenta against the samples' aubergine (1600: X shapes beside the sconces; 1280: shafts almost vanish).

The moonlight ends as soft spotlight cones that fade into a void floor, and the parchment and option strips have clean straight edges like a styled panel (1600: cones end in nothing; 1280: same, with an even rectangular page).

The moonlight reads as a sheer curtain and the wall and wainscot above the flagstone pools stay very dark, so only the page and floor feel painted (1600: veil shape beside the sconces; 1280: thin dark cracks cross the bright pools).

The central niche has no edge and fades into blackness, while the ribbon-tailed trick rows have heavy gold ends that compete with the card (1600: columns dissolve at the top; 1280: tails crowd the panel edge).

The thin columns barely frame the card, the FROM YOUR FINAL DECK plaque is too narrow for its words, and the trick rows are blurred purple smears in plain boxes (1600: niche lost in the wall; 1280: plaque lettering touches its ends).

The central niche stops at hard rectangular edges like a pasted image, with flat cream cost and row badges and plaque lettering biting the cartouche ends (1600: box edge at both sides of the niche; 1280: FROM and DECK touch the plaque ends).

The pinkish-brown leather rules panel is lighter and flatter than everything around the card, so it pulls the eye from the art, though the arched niche holds well (1600: panel reads as a pasted swatch; 1280: wide plaque stays clean but the panel still jumps).

The cost disks are dark, plain counters that barely register as struck metal, and the large near-empty navy rules panels are the deadest surface on the wares (1600: wide unused panel area; 1280: same, with legible numerals).

Mr. Moth's nameplate floats on the curtain below the shelf, cut off from his portrait, and the rules panels stay big dark voids (1600: plaque sits alone in the gap above the strip; 1280: it overlaps the shelf end without attaching).

Flat cream cost disks look like web badges against the worn card frames, and Mr. Moth's nameplate straddles a dark shelf block with its lower line on the edge (1600: subtitle sits on the shelf edge; 1280: plaque crosses the block; TRICKS banner lettering is faint at both).

The cost numerals are too dim against their worn rims, and the even mid-blue leather rules panels read flatter and bluer than the card frames (1600: the 2 and 1 sink into their disks; 1280: numerals dimmer still, though legible).

The condition plaques float beside the actors with no fixing to the room, and their coloured glow lettering is still cooler than the candlelight (1600: top-row plaques crowd Maya's head; 1280: stacked columns read cleanly).
The condition plaques are plain gold-outlined rectangles that read closest to web tags, abandoning the cartouche shape used on the Butler title and HUD (obvious at both 1600 and 1280).

The condition lettering sits on bright violet grounds in near-neon pink and cyan, so it floats above the warm room instead of being lit by it (1600: Strength and Vulnerable glow; 1280: violet plaque grounds stand out more).

The warm engraved plaque lettering belongs to the room, but its plus signs and letterforms are low contrast against the plaque (1600: the plus signs nearly vanish; 1280: Strength and Bristle are the hardest to read at a glance).

winner_fixes: gameover, central niche: replace the thin columns that dissolve into the wall with a substantial arched alcove whose gold-edged top and warm wood clearly frame the card.
combat-floaters, plaques beside both actors: replace the plain gold rectangles with the same ended cartouche shape used on the Butler title and HUD, keeping the large lettering.
gameover, right-hand trick rows: replace the blurred purple smears with a crisp painted enamel or velvet ground and engraved row ends, so they match the gold cost medallions.
gameover, FROM YOUR FINAL DECK plaque: widen it under the card so the lettering clears the cartouche ends at both 1600x900 and 1280x800.
event, moonlight on both sides: strengthen the shafts and remove the muddy X crossings, so one readable window shape runs from each window down the wainscot into its floor pool.
event and rest, upper walls: pull the damask from magenta toward the samples' aubergine, especially at the right edge and around the title cartouche, while keeping the pattern visible.
shop, Mr. Moth's nameplate: attach it to something, by hanging it from the shelf lip on small chains or setting it into a carved bracket, instead of floating it on the curtain.
rest, lower-left floor: bring the rug's red and blue down into the candle-lit range and repaint the harsh striped strip at the bottom-left so floor and wainscot share one light.
event, parchment edges: deckle the left, right and lower sides to match the burned top edge, and vary the burn on the option strips so the sheet reads as one damaged object.
shop, card rules panels: give the large dark voids a painted surface with visible grain and worn corners, without reducing the large text.

grafts.idea: Use the gameover arched niche with its gold-lit top and warm wood columns as the card's setting.
Use the event parchment's deckled silhouette, paler aged centre and heavier curling bookmark, which make the page the best single object in the round.
Use the wider FROM YOUR FINAL DECK plaque, which clears its lettering at both sizes.
Borrow the textured rules-panel idea for shop cards, but darken and desaturate the leather so it sits with the card frames instead of reading as a pasted swatch.
Use the condition-plaque cartouches and their lettering balance in combat: ornamented, warm-edged and still instantly readable at 1280x800.
Use a restrained version of the window-mullion shadow inside Jasper's event shafts and floor pools, so the light clearly comes from the windows.

verdicts.verdict: JASPER is the winner, but no candidate fits between the samples: none reaches coherence 9 or a score near the painted-hand bar. It wins because its damask, wainscot, table, rug and floors build an actual room on rest and event, and its gold cost disks and shop wall are the richest. Its failures are local and graftable: a weak gameover niche, smeared rows, a tight plaque and rectangular combat plaques. MALACHITE was a close second and has the best individual objects, including the parchment, arched niche and pedestal, but its rooms stay darker and its cost numerals and combat plus signs lose contrast. CITRINE has the best combat plaques but flatter rooms and pasted-looking moonlight. SERPENTINE ranks last or near last on every screen because of its void floors, spotlight cones, hard niche edges and flat cream badges. At 1280x800 all four keep large text legible; the differences are JASPER's and SERPENTINE's tight gameover plaque, MALACHITE's dim disks and plaque lettering, and SERPENTINE's and JASPER's unattached shop nameplates.
